definition: The work that must be done, and the results that must be delivered, for the project to be complete.
wrongs: Every idea anyone mentions, whether or not it was agreed.
Only the project manager's personal tasks, excluding deliverables.
The company's entire strategy for the next decade.
why: Scope is the agreed boundary of work and deliverables that defines completion.
example: The scope of a campus app covers student timetables but excludes fee payments, which stay in another system.
scenario: Stakeholders argue about whether fee payments belong in a timetable app. Which statement should settle the argument?
scenarioWrongs: The loudest new idea in the latest meeting
The project manager's private to-do list
The company's ten-year strategy in full
scenarioWhy: Project scope is the agreed work and deliverables, so it decides whether fee payments are included.

definition: A document that describes the project's deliverables, acceptance boundaries, and what is explicitly excluded.
wrongs: A blank Gantt chart with no description of deliverables.
A list of every employee's hobbies.
A verbal hope that the team will know what to build.
why: A scope statement writes down deliverables, boundaries, and exclusions so the agreement can be checked later.
example: The statement says the portal will show grades and explicitly excludes online payment.
scenario: A sponsor later asks for online payment. The team needs the written inclusions and exclusions. Which document is that?
scenarioWrongs: A blank Gantt chart
A list of hobbies
An unwritten hope about the build
scenarioWhy: The scope statement records deliverables and explicit exclusions such as online payment.

definition: Uncontrolled growth of work or deliverables without a corresponding approved change to time, cost, or resources.
wrongs: An approved change that adds time and budget for the new work.
Removing a feature so the team can finish on the original date.
Writing the original scope before any work starts.
why: Scope creep is uncontrolled addition of work, unlike a change that is approved with matching time or cost.
example: Designers keep adding unapproved report screens, and the launch date slips with no extra budget.
scenario: Extra report screens are added every week with no approval and no extra time. Which problem is that?
scenarioWrongs: An approved change with added budget
Cutting a feature to protect the date
Writing the original scope
scenarioWhy: Uncontrolled extra work without approved time or cost is scope creep.

definition: A hierarchical breakdown of the project scope into smaller, manageable components of work.
wrongs: A calendar that only shows dates and hides the work components.
An organisation chart of the whole company, unrelated to this project's deliverables.
A risk list sorted by probability.
why: A work breakdown structure decomposes scope into smaller components so work can be estimated and assigned.
example: The campus-app scope is broken into registration, timetable view, notifications, and project management.
scenario: The team needs the scope split into smaller pieces before estimating. Which artefact should they build?
scenarioWrongs: A calendar with dates only
The company organisation chart
A risk list sorted by probability
scenarioWhy: A work breakdown structure is the hierarchy that decomposes scope into manageable components.

definition: The lowest-level component in the work breakdown structure that can be estimated, assigned, and tracked.
wrongs: The whole project treated as one lump with no owner.
A milestone diamond that marks a date but contains no work.
A stakeholder's job title outside the project.
why: A work package is a leaf of the breakdown that is small enough to estimate, assign, and control.
example: Build the timetable export is assigned to one developer, estimated at 40 hours, and tracked to done.
scenario: One developer will own a 40-hour piece of the timetable export, tracked to completion. Which label fits that piece?
scenarioWrongs: The entire project as one lump
A milestone with no work content
A stakeholder job title
scenarioWhy: A work package is the lowest breakdown item that can be estimated, assigned, and tracked.

definition: A tangible or verifiable product, result, or capability that must be produced to complete part of the project.
wrongs: A private intention that produces nothing others can check.
The number of meetings held, regardless of output.
A team member's years of experience.
why: A deliverable is an output others can verify, not effort, meetings, or experience by themselves.
example: The tested login module handed to the sponsor is a deliverable; the hours spent writing it are not.
scenario: The sponsor asks what they will be able to inspect at the next review. Which item is a deliverable?
scenarioWrongs: The number of meetings held
A private intention with no output
A developer's years of experience
scenarioWhy: A deliverable is a verifiable product such as the tested login module, not meetings or experience.

definition: The conditions a deliverable must meet before the customer or sponsor agrees to accept it.
wrongs: The project manager's private feeling that the work is good enough.
The date the work happened to finish.
The brand of laptop used to build it.
why: Acceptance criteria are the agreed conditions that define when a deliverable is fit to accept.
example: The search feature is accepted only if it returns results within two seconds on the agreed test set.
scenario: The sponsor will accept search only if results return within two seconds on the agreed tests. Which term names those conditions?
scenarioWrongs: A private feeling that it looks fine
The date the coding happened to end
The laptop brand
scenarioWhy: Acceptance criteria are the agreed conditions, such as the two-second test, that govern acceptance.

definition: A distinct piece of scheduled work that consumes time and usually resources, and that helps produce a deliverable.
wrongs: A point in time with zero duration that only marks an event.
The name of the sponsoring department.
A risk that might happen later.
why: An activity is work with duration on the schedule, unlike a milestone, which is a zero-duration marker.
example: Write the user guide is scheduled for five days and assigned to the technical author.
scenario: Write the user guide takes five days and is placed on the schedule. Which schedule element is it?
scenarioWrongs: A zero-duration milestone
The sponsoring department's name
A risk that may occur later
scenarioWhy: Scheduled work that consumes time, such as five days of writing, is an activity.

definition: A zero-duration marker on the schedule that represents a significant event, such as an approval or a handover.
wrongs: A five-day task in which someone writes a guide.
The total budget of the project.
A team member's hourly rate.
why: A milestone marks an event and has no duration of its own, unlike an activity.
example: Sponsor approval of the design is shown as a diamond on the date of the review, with no length of its own.
scenario: The schedule must mark the day the sponsor approves the design, without giving that marker a duration. Which element is used?
scenarioWrongs: A five-day writing activity
The project budget
An hourly pay rate
scenarioWhy: A milestone is a zero-duration marker for a significant event such as design approval.

definition: A bar chart that shows activities against a timescale, including their start, finish, and often their dependencies.
wrongs: A hierarchy of scope components with no dates.
A list of risks and their owners.
A pie chart of the company share price.
why: A Gantt chart displays schedule information as bars on a calendar, which a scope hierarchy does not.
example: The chart shows testing as a two-week bar starting only after the build bar ends.
scenario: The sponsor wants to see activity bars on a calendar, including which work starts after build. Which chart fits?
scenarioWrongs: A work breakdown with no dates
A risk list
A share-price pie chart
scenarioWhy: A Gantt chart shows activities as bars on a timescale, including when one follows another.

definition: A graph of activities and their logical dependencies, used to find the paths through the schedule.
wrongs: A drawing of the office computer cables.
A bar chart whose main feature is a calendar axis rather than logic paths.
An organisation chart of line managers.
why: A network diagram shows logical dependencies among activities so paths, including the critical path, can be analysed.
example: The diagram shows that training cannot start until both the software and the handbook are finished.
scenario: The team must see that training waits on both the software and the handbook. Which diagram shows that logic?
scenarioWrongs: A drawing of office cables
An organisation chart
A pie chart of costs
scenarioWhy: A network diagram shows logical dependencies, such as training waiting on two predecessors.

definition: A logical relationship in which one activity cannot start or finish until another activity has reached a required state.
wrongs: Two tasks that merely share the same week by coincidence.
A personal friendship between two team members.
A preference for working near a window.
why: A dependency is a logical constraint between activities, not a coincidence of dates or a personal preference.
example: User testing depends on the test environment being ready, so testing is linked as a successor.
scenario: User testing cannot start until the test environment is ready. Which relationship should the schedule record?
scenarioWrongs: A coincidental shared week
A friendship between testers
A preference for a window seat
scenarioWhy: A logical link that stops testing until the environment is ready is a dependency.

definition: An overlap that allows a successor activity to start before its predecessor has finished.
wrongs: A required wait inserted after a predecessor finishes before the successor may start.
The person who manages the schedule.
The total length of the critical path.
why: Lead is an overlap that accelerates a successor, whereas lag is a delay between activities.
example: Writing the guide starts five days before coding finishes, shown as a lead on that link.
scenario: The guide may start five days before coding finishes. Which schedule feature records that overlap?
scenarioWrongs: A required wait after coding ends
The person who owns the schedule
The length of the critical path
scenarioWhy: An overlap that lets the successor start early is a lead, not a waiting lag.

definition: A required delay between a predecessor and its successor, so the successor waits after the predecessor reaches the linked point.
wrongs: An overlap that lets the successor start early.
Free time that an activity can slip without affecting the project finish.
The name of the scheduling tool.
why: Lag is a deliberate delay on a dependency, not spare float and not an accelerating overlap.
example: Paint must dry for two days after plastering, so a two-day lag is placed before decorating starts.
scenario: Decorating must wait two days after plastering so the surface can dry. Which feature records that wait?
scenarioWrongs: An overlap that starts decorating early
Spare float on an unrelated task
The brand name of the scheduling tool
scenarioWhy: A required wait between predecessor and successor is lag.

definition: The longest path of dependent activities through the schedule, whose delay delays the project finish.
wrongs: The shortest list of easy tasks that can all slip without moving the end date.
The path the project manager walks to the meeting room.
Any task the sponsor mentions first in a meeting.
why: The critical path is the longest dependent chain, so it determines the earliest finish and has no spare time.
example: Design, build, and test form a 30-day chain, longer than any other path, so that chain sets the finish date.
scenario: Design, build, and test form the longest chain and set the finish date. Which label applies to that chain?
scenarioWrongs: A set of tasks that can all slip freely
The walk to the meeting room
Whichever task was mentioned first
scenarioWhy: The longest dependent chain, which sets the project finish, is the critical path.

definition: The time an activity can be delayed without delaying the project finish date.
wrongs: The time an activity can slip before it delays only its immediate successor, even if the project end is safe.
The amount of money left in the budget.
The number of people who are free this afternoon.
why: Total float is slack relative to the project finish date, and critical activities have none.
example: Documentation can slip three days and the go-live date still holds, so its total float is three days.
scenario: Documentation can slip three days without moving go-live. Which measure is three days?
scenarioWrongs: Money left in the budget
The number of free people
The full project duration
scenarioWhy: Total float is how long an activity can slip without delaying the project finish.

definition: The approved version of the schedule against which actual progress and changes are compared.
wrongs: A rough sketch that nobody has approved and that changes silently each day.
The list of risks that might affect dates.
A photo of the team on the first day.
why: The schedule baseline is the approved plan used as the reference for measuring delay and approving date changes.
example: Progress reports compare actual finish dates with the baseline approved at the kickoff.
scenario: Reports must show delay against the dates the sponsor approved at kickoff. Which version of the schedule is the reference?
scenarioWrongs: An unapproved sketch that changes daily
The risk list
The team photograph
scenarioWhy: The schedule baseline is the approved schedule used to compare actual progress.

definition: An uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive or negative effect on project objectives.
wrongs: A problem that has already happened and now needs action.
A fact that is already known and certain.
The project title printed on the cover.
why: A risk is uncertain and may help or harm objectives, whereas an issue is a problem that has already occurred.
example: A key supplier might miss the component date, which would delay build if it happens.
scenario: A supplier might miss a component date, but it has not happened yet. Which label fits?
scenarioWrongs: An issue that has already occurred
A certain fact already known
The project title
scenarioWhy: An uncertain event that could affect objectives is a risk until it actually occurs.

definition: A living log of identified risks, their ratings, owners, and planned responses.
wrongs: A diary of problems that have already happened, with no uncertain events.
The approved budget spreadsheet.
A contact list with no risks recorded.
why: The risk register is where identified risks, ratings, owners, and responses are recorded and updated.
example: The register lists a late supplier, rates it high, names the procurement lead, and records a backup vendor.
scenario: The team must record a late-supplier threat, its rating, its owner, and the backup-vendor response. Which log is used?
scenarioWrongs: A diary of past problems only
The budget spreadsheet
A contact list with no risks
scenarioWhy: The risk register logs identified risks together with ratings, owners, and responses.

definition: The two ratings commonly used to judge a risk: how likely it is, and how severe the effect would be if it occurred.
wrongs: The start date and finish date of a task.
The first name and surname of the sponsor.
The font size and colour of a slide.
why: Risk rating combines likelihood and severity so the team can prioritise responses.
example: A data-loss threat is rated likely and severe, so it is prioritised above a rare and mild documentation delay.
scenario: Two threats must be prioritised. One is likely and severe; the other is rare and mild. Which pair of ratings supports that ranking?
scenarioWrongs: Start date and finish date
The sponsor's names
Font size and colour
scenarioWhy: Probability and impact rate how likely a risk is and how severe it would be, which drives priority.

definition: A response that reduces the probability or the impact of a threat.
wrongs: A response that removes the risky work entirely so the threat cannot occur.
A response that shifts the financial effect to an insurer and leaves the event unchanged.
Doing nothing and accepting the threat as it stands.
why: Mitigation lowers likelihood or impact but does not necessarily eliminate the activity or transfer the loss.
example: The team adds a second supplier so a delay is less likely, while still buying the same component.
scenario: The team keeps the component but adds a second supplier to make delay less likely. Which response is that?
scenarioWrongs: Dropping the component so the threat disappears
Insuring the loss and changing nothing else
Accepting the threat with no action
scenarioWhy: Reducing the likelihood of delay while continuing the work is mitigation.

definition: A response that removes a threat by changing the plan so the risky activity is no longer done.
wrongs: Reducing the chance of a threat while still doing the same activity.
Buying insurance so someone else pays if the threat occurs.
Keeping the plan unchanged and accepting the threat.
why: Avoidance eliminates exposure by changing the plan, rather than merely reducing or transferring the risk.
example: The team drops a risky third-party login and uses the university account so that threat no longer exists.
scenario: To eliminate a risky third-party login, the team removes that approach from the plan. Which response is that?
scenarioWrongs: Keeping the login but adding monitoring
Insuring the login and leaving it in place
Accepting the risky login unchanged
scenarioWhy: Changing the plan so the risky activity is not done is risk avoidance.

definition: A response that shifts the financial impact of a threat to a third party, such as through insurance or a contract clause.
wrongs: Removing the risky work from the project entirely.
Adding tests so the threat is less likely, while the team still bears the loss.
Ignoring the threat because it feels unlikely.
why: Transfer moves the financial consequence to another party; it does not remove the event or automatically reduce its chance.
example: The contract makes the vendor pay agreed damages if their hosted service misses the uptime target.
scenario: The vendor must pay damages if uptime is missed, while the service stays in the plan. Which response is that?
scenarioWrongs: Removing the service from the project
Adding tests while the team still pays for any loss
Ignoring the uptime threat
scenarioWhy: Shifting the financial impact to the vendor by contract is risk transfer.

definition: The risk that remains after the planned responses have been applied.
wrongs: The risk as it was before any response was chosen.
A brand-new risk created by the response itself.
A problem that has already occurred.
why: Residual risk is what is left of a threat once the chosen responses are in place.
example: After a backup supplier is added, a small chance of delay remains because both suppliers share one port.
scenario: A backup supplier is in place, yet a small chance of delay remains. Which label fits that remaining chance?
scenarioWrongs: The original risk before any response
A new risk created by the response
An outage that happened yesterday
scenarioWhy: Risk left after the planned response is applied is residual risk.

definition: A problem or decision that has already arisen and now needs action, rather than an uncertainty about the future.
wrongs: An uncertain event that might affect the project if it occurs later.
A milestone that was completed successfully.
A benefit the sponsor hopes to gain.
why: An issue is current and requires action, whereas a risk is still uncertain.
example: The test server failed this morning, so the team logs an issue and assigns someone to restore it.
scenario: The test server failed this morning and work is blocked. Which item should the team log?
scenarioWrongs: A risk that might happen next month
A milestone already completed
A hoped-for benefit
scenarioWhy: A problem that has already happened and needs action is an issue, not a future risk.

definition: A person or group that can affect the project or that is affected by its decisions or results.
wrongs: Only people named on the project payroll.
A person with neither influence nor any effect from the result.
The file format used for the schedule.
why: Project stakeholders include anyone who influences the work or who is affected by it, not only paid team members.
example: Students who will use a campus app are stakeholders even though they are not on the project team.
scenario: Students will use the campus app but are not paid team members. How should the project treat them?
scenarioWrongs: As people who can be ignored
As members of the paid project team
As a file format
scenarioWhy: People affected by the result are project stakeholders even when they are not on the payroll.

definition: A document that records stakeholders, their interests, influence, and the approach for engaging them.
wrongs: A Gantt chart of activity dates.
A list of source-code files.
A budget broken down by cost type.
why: The stakeholder register captures who matters, what they care about, and how the project will engage them.
example: The register lists the registrar as high influence, interested in data privacy, and to be consulted monthly.
scenario: The team needs each stakeholder's influence, interest, and engagement approach in one place. Which document is that?
scenarioWrongs: The Gantt chart
The source-code list
The cost budget
scenarioWhy: The stakeholder register records stakeholders together with interest, influence, and engagement.

definition: A document that states what project information each audience needs, in what form, how often, and from whom.
wrongs: A plan that only lists the technical tasks and their durations.
A single unplanned message sent during a crisis, with no agreed pattern.
A wiring diagram for the office network.
why: A communication plan sets the audience, content, format, frequency, and sender for project information.
example: The plan says students get a monthly plain-language update by email, written by the project manager.
scenario: Students should get a monthly plain-language email from the project manager. Which document records that agreement?
scenarioWrongs: The activity duration list
One unplanned crisis text
The network wiring diagram
scenarioWhy: The communication plan specifies audience, content, form, frequency, and sender.

definition: A grid that assigns, for each task or decision, who is responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed.
wrongs: A chart of activity bars on a calendar.
A list of risks sorted by score.
A budget of labour hours with no roles.
why: RACI clarifies the four participation roles so each task has a clear doer and a single accountable owner.
example: For the privacy review, the analyst is responsible, the sponsor is accountable, legal is consulted, and the team is informed.
scenario: A privacy review needs one doer, one accountable owner, a legal consultee, and a team to notify. Which grid records that?
scenarioWrongs: A Gantt chart
A scored risk list
A labour-hour budget
scenarioWhy: A RACI matrix assigns responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed roles for a task.

definition: A regular project update that compares progress with the plan and highlights issues, risks, and decisions needed.
wrongs: The original charter that authorised the project.
A celebration email that hides a known delay.
The final lessons-learned note written after closure.
why: A status report is a recurring comparison of actual progress with the plan, including problems that need attention.
example: Friday's report shows testing is three days behind baseline and asks the sponsor to decide on overtime.
scenario: Testing is three days behind the approved dates and a decision on overtime is needed. Which update should the sponsor receive?
scenarioAnswer: A status report comparing progress with the plan
scenarioWrongs: The original charter only
A celebration note that hides the delay
The closure lessons, which do not exist yet
scenarioWhy: A status report compares progress with the plan and raises the decision the sponsor must make.

definition: The meeting that starts coordinated execution by aligning the team and stakeholders on goals, roles, and near-term work.
wrongs: The meeting that closes the project and archives the files.
A private lunch with no discussion of goals or roles.
The interview that hired the project manager months earlier.
why: Kickoff aligns people on purpose, roles, and the first work as execution begins.
example: At kickoff the sponsor states the go-live date, the team confirms roles, and the first sprint goal is agreed.
scenario: Execution is about to start and the team must align on the date, roles, and first goal. Which meeting is that?
scenarioWrongs: The closure meeting
A private lunch with no project content
The hiring interview from months ago
scenarioWhy: The kickoff meeting aligns team and stakeholders as coordinated execution starts.

definition: An estimate based on the actual cost or duration of a similar past project, adjusted for known differences.
wrongs: An estimate built by summing detailed estimates of every small work package.
An estimate produced from a statistical rate times a measured quantity.
A guess with no reference to any past project.
why: Analogous estimating uses a similar historical project as the base and then adjusts it.
example: Last year's similar app took 12 weeks, and this one adds a week because it has one extra integration.
scenario: Last year's similar app took 12 weeks, and this one has one extra integration worth about a week. Which estimating approach is being used?
scenarioWrongs: Summing estimates of every work package
Multiplying a rate by a measured quantity
Guessing with no past project
scenarioWhy: Using a similar past duration and adjusting for a known difference is analogous estimating.

definition: An estimate produced by applying a statistical rate, such as hours per screen, to a measured quantity of work.
wrongs: An estimate copied from one similar past project and then adjusted.
An estimate formed from optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic figures.
An estimate that adds up individually estimated work packages.
why: Parametric estimating multiplies a known rate by a quantity, rather than copying one whole past project.
example: Historical data show 6 hours per report, and 10 reports imply an estimate of 60 hours.
scenario: History shows 6 hours per report, and there are 10 reports. Which method produces the 60-hour estimate?
scenarioWrongs: Copying one past project and adjusting it
Averaging optimistic and pessimistic guesses only
Adding up each package with no rate
scenarioWhy: Applying a rate of hours per report to a count of reports is parametric estimating.

definition: An estimating technique that uses optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic figures to produce an expected value.
wrongs: A single figure copied from one past project.
A rate multiplied by a quantity, with no range of outcomes.
The average of three people's favourite numbers, unrelated to the work.
why: Three-point estimating recognises uncertainty by combining optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic values.
example: Coding is judged at 4, 6, and 14 days, and the expected duration uses those three figures.
scenario: The team has optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic durations for coding and wants one expected value. Which technique fits?
scenarioWrongs: Copying a single past duration
Multiplying one rate by a quantity
Averaging numbers that are unrelated to the work
scenarioWhy: Combining optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic figures into an expected value is three-point estimating.

definition: An estimate built by estimating the lowest work packages in detail and summing them to higher levels.
wrongs: An estimate taken from one similar project without looking at the packages.
A rate applied to a single total quantity with no package detail.
A sponsor's target date imposed with no estimate of the work.
why: Bottom-up estimating starts at detailed packages and adds them up, which takes effort but is more specific.
example: Each of eight work packages is estimated, and the total of 26 days becomes the phase estimate.
scenario: Eight work packages are estimated separately and then added to get the phase total. Which method is that?
scenarioWrongs: Using one similar project with no package detail
Applying one rate to a single quantity
Adopting a target date with no estimate
scenarioWhy: Summing detailed estimates of the lowest work packages is bottom-up estimating.

definition: The amount of labour required to complete an activity, often measured in person-hours, independent of calendar time.
wrongs: The number of calendar days from start to finish, regardless of how many people work.
The money charged by a vendor for a licence.
The emotional energy of a meeting.
why: Effort measures labour content, while duration measures elapsed calendar time.
example: A review needs 16 person-hours, which two people can finish in one calendar day.
scenario: A review needs 16 person-hours. Two people are available. Which figure is the 16 person-hours?
scenarioWrongs: The calendar duration of one day
The vendor licence fee
The number of slides in the review
scenarioWhy: Person-hours of labour are effort, whereas the one calendar day is duration.

definition: The amount of calendar time between the start and finish of an activity, given the resources assigned.
wrongs: The total person-hours, ignoring how those hours are spread across days.
The project budget in money.
The count of stakeholders.
why: Duration is elapsed calendar time, which depends on how effort is staffed.
example: Sixteen person-hours staffed by two people has a duration of one working day.
scenario: Sixteen person-hours are staffed with two people and finish in one working day. Which figure is that one day?
scenarioWrongs: The 16 person-hours of effort
The project budget
The number of stakeholders
scenarioWhy: Duration is the calendar time from start to finish once staffing is taken into account.

definition: Time or money held inside the project baseline to cover identified risks that may occur.
wrongs: A reserve kept by senior management for unknown unknowns, outside the project baseline.
Money already spent on completed work.
The profit the vendor hopes to make.
why: Contingency reserve covers known risks and sits in the baseline; it is not management reserve for unidentified uncertainty.
example: The schedule includes three contingency days because a known permit risk may delay installation.
scenario: A known permit risk may delay installation, so the baseline includes three extra days for that risk. Which reserve is that?
scenarioWrongs: Money already spent
The vendor's hoped-for profit
A senior reserve for risks nobody has identified
scenarioWhy: Time held in the baseline for an identified risk is contingency reserve.

definition: Deciding the quality standards for the project and how the team will meet them.
wrongs: Inspecting a finished deliverable to count defects.
Auditing whether the team followed its quality process.
Choosing the office paint colour with no link to deliverables.
why: Quality planning sets the standards and the approach before execution and inspection.
example: The plan states that each release must pass the agreed accessibility checklist before demonstration.
scenario: Before build, the team agrees that every release must pass an accessibility checklist. Which process is that agreement part of?
scenarioWrongs: Counting defects in a finished build
Auditing whether the process was followed
Choosing paint for the office
scenarioWhy: Deciding the standards and how they will be met, before the work, is quality planning.

definition: Checking that the project's quality processes are being followed so defects are less likely to be created.
wrongs: Inspecting a deliverable against standards to find defects in that product.
Writing the quality standards for the first time.
Cancelling all reviews to save time.
why: Quality assurance evaluates the process, whereas quality control inspects the product.
example: An auditor checks that code reviews required by the quality plan actually took place this sprint.
scenario: An auditor checks that required code reviews happened, rather than retesting the product. Which activity is that?
scenarioWrongs: Inspecting the product for defects
Writing the standards for the first time
Cancelling reviews
scenarioWhy: Checking that quality processes were followed is quality assurance, not an inspection of the product.

definition: Inspecting deliverables against standards to find defects and confirm whether acceptance conditions are met.
wrongs: Auditing whether people followed the quality process, without looking at the product.
Choosing which standards will apply next year.
Ignoring test results so the date can be met.
why: Quality control examines the deliverable itself and compares it with the standard or acceptance conditions.
example: Testers run the accessibility checklist on the release and log two failures before the demo.
scenario: Testers run the checklist on the release and log failures in the product. Which activity is that?
scenarioWrongs: Auditing that meetings were held, without looking at the product
Choosing next year's standards
Ignoring the failures to protect the date
scenarioWhy: Inspecting the deliverable against the checklist is quality control.

definition: A formal proposal to modify an approved baseline, such as scope, schedule, or cost, so the change can be assessed.
wrongs: A silent edit to the baseline with no record.
A suggestion shouted in a corridor and then forgotten.
The original approved scope itself.
why: A change request makes a proposed baseline change visible so impact can be assessed and a decision recorded.
example: The sponsor submits a request to add fee payments, and the team estimates two extra weeks before any approval.
scenario: The sponsor wants fee payments added after the baseline was approved. Which item should be raised before the work starts?
scenarioWrongs: A silent edit to the baseline
A forgotten corridor comment
The original scope with no modification
scenarioWhy: A formal change request lets the team assess a proposed change to the approved baseline before acting.

definition: An approved version of a plan, such as scope, schedule, or cost, used as the reference for measuring performance.
wrongs: A draft that changes whenever someone has a new idea and has never been approved.
The actual results after the work is finished.
A stakeholder's personal opinion of quality.
why: A baseline is the approved reference; performance is measured by comparing actual results with it.
example: Cost reports compare actual spend with the cost baseline approved by the sponsor.
scenario: Cost reports must show variance from the spend figure the sponsor approved. Which figure is that reference?
scenarioWrongs: An unapproved draft that changes daily
The actual spend after the fact
A personal opinion of quality
scenarioWhy: The baseline is the approved reference against which actual performance is compared.

definition: A document issued by the sponsor that authorises the project and states its purpose, manager, and high-level constraints.
wrongs: A detailed schedule of every activity and dependency.
A test log of defects found in the last build.
A vendor invoice for completed work.
why: The charter authorises the project at a high level; it is not the detailed schedule or a test record.
example: The dean signs a charter naming the student portal, the project manager, the budget cap, and the June goal.
scenario: The team needs written authority to start, including the manager, purpose, and budget cap. Which document provides that?
scenarioWrongs: A detailed activity network
A defect log
A vendor invoice
scenarioWhy: The project charter is the sponsor's authorisation, naming purpose, manager, and high-level constraints.

definition: The person who provides authority and resources for the project and is accountable for its business outcome.
wrongs: A contractor who only installs equipment and cannot approve scope.
A team member who writes code but does not own the business result.
A tool that stores the schedule.
why: The sponsor champions the project, supplies resources, and answers for the business result.
example: The registrar sponsors the enrolment project, approves its scope changes, and owns the promised reduction in queues.
scenario: Someone must approve scope changes and answer for shorter enrolment queues. Which role is that?
scenarioWrongs: A contractor who only installs equipment
A developer with no authority over scope
The scheduling tool
scenarioWhy: The project sponsor provides authority and resources and is accountable for the business outcome.

definition: The linked limits of scope, time, and cost, where changing one usually forces a change in at least one of the others.
wrongs: Three unrelated office rules about dress, parking, and email.
A claim that scope, time, and cost can all be fixed while work is freely added.
The three names of the steering-group chairs.
why: The triple constraint describes the trade-off among scope, time, and cost on a project.
example: Adding fee payments without moving the date forces either more budget or a cut somewhere else in scope.
scenario: The sponsor adds features but will not move the date or the budget. Which concept explains why that combination is unrealistic?
scenarioWrongs: Office rules on dress and parking
A claim that extra scope is free
The names of three chairs
scenarioWhy: The triple constraint means extra scope usually requires more time or cost, so all three cannot stay fixed.

definition: Recorded knowledge from what went well and what did not, captured so later work can reuse it.
wrongs: A blame list that names people but records no reusable knowledge.
The original business case, unchanged at the end.
A deleted mailbox with no notes kept.
why: Lessons learned turn project experience into knowledge the next piece of work can use.
example: The team records that late hardware orders caused delay, and the next project orders hardware at kickoff.
scenario: Late hardware orders caused delay, and the next project should avoid that. Which record should carry that knowledge forward?
scenarioWrongs: A blame list with no reusable point
The unchanged original business case
A deleted mailbox
scenarioWhy: Lessons learned capture what happened and how later work should change, such as ordering hardware earlier.

definition: A record of factors treated as true for planning purposes, which are checked because they may be wrong.
wrongs: A list of uncertain events with probability and impact.
A list of problems that have already happened.
A catalogue of office furniture.
why: Assumptions are planning premises treated as true, and the log makes them visible so they can be validated.
example: The plan assumes the test lab is free in May, and that assumption is logged and later confirmed with the lab owner.
scenario: The schedule assumes the test lab is free in May, but nobody has confirmed it. Where should that premise be recorded and checked?
scenarioWrongs: Only in a risk register as if it were already an event
In an issue log before anything is wrong
In a furniture catalogue
scenarioWhy: A planning premise treated as true, and still needing confirmation, belongs in the assumptions log.

definition: Shortening the schedule by adding resources to critical activities, usually at extra cost.
wrongs: Overlapping activities that were planned in sequence, without adding resources.
Lengthening the schedule to reduce cost.
Removing scope so the date can be met with the same team.
why: Crashing trades cost for time by adding resources on the critical path.
example: A second developer is added to the critical build task so it finishes a week earlier at higher labour cost.
scenario: The critical build must finish a week sooner, and the sponsor will pay for another developer. Which technique is that?
scenarioWrongs: Overlapping tasks without extra people
Extending the date to save money
Cutting scope and keeping the same team
scenarioWhy: Adding paid resources to shorten critical work is crashing.

definition: Shortening the schedule by overlapping activities that were originally planned to run in sequence, which increases risk.
wrongs: Adding people to a critical task so it finishes sooner at higher cost.
Inserting a delay between two activities.
Accepting a later finish date.
why: Fast tracking overlaps sequential work to save calendar time and typically raises the chance of rework.
example: Testing starts before coding is fully finished, saving a week but risking retests when late changes arrive.
scenario: Testing will start before coding finishes to save a week, accepting more rework risk. Which technique is that?
scenarioWrongs: Adding paid staff to the same task
Inserting a waiting lag
Moving the finish date later
scenarioWhy: Overlapping work that was sequential, in order to shorten the schedule, is fast tracking.
